work_or_witness: Māori Mythology · ‘Ngā atua – the gods’, opening and §§ ‘Rangi, Papa and their children’ and ‘Other supernatural beings’, paras. 1–3
definition: Te Ara identifies atua as central to Māori religion and uses ‘gods’ as an English gloss; its creation reference calls Tāne an atua (divine presence).
cultural_caution: Do not treat atua as a standardized fantasy pantheon, a species, or an exact equivalent of ‘god’; relationships, names, and meanings are witness- and community-specific.

citations.locator: ‘Ngā atua – the gods’, opening and §§ ‘Rangi, Papa and their children’ and ‘Other supernatural beings’, paras. 1–3
supports: The page defines its English framing of atua and distinguishes atua, tipua, and taniwha.

work_or_witness: ‘What are taniwha?’, §§ ‘A creature of many forms’ and ‘Taniwha and chiefs’, paras. 1–4
definition: Supernatural beings whose forms and characteristics vary according to different tribal traditions; the cited reference says they were understood as part of the natural environment and may be protective or dangerous.
cultural_caution: ‘Dragon’ and ‘monster’ are descriptions reported by Te Ara, not equivalents. Do not flatten taniwha into a creature class or detach a named taniwha from its iwi/hapū and landscape relations.

citations.locator: ‘What are taniwha?’, §§ ‘A creature of many forms’ and ‘Taniwha and chiefs’, paras. 1–4
supports: Forms and characteristics vary according to tribal traditions; taniwha can be connected to protective relations and landscape.

work_or_witness: Māori Mythology · ‘What is whakapapa?’, opening and §§ ‘Types of whakapapa’ and ‘Uses of different recitations’, paras. 1–8
definition: A framework linking animate and inanimate, known and unknown phenomena in terrestrial and spiritual worlds; Te Ara says it organizes, preserves, and transmits relationships, knowledge, tikanga, philosophies, and spiritualities.
cultural_caution: Do not reduce whakapapa to a fantasy family-tree mechanic, ancestry stat, or database provenance field. It is living mātauranga and varies in use, recitation, and authority.

citations.locator: ‘What is whakapapa?’, opening and §§ ‘Types of whakapapa’ and ‘Uses of different recitations’, paras. 1–8
supports: Whakapapa is described as a framework of relationships and core traditional mātauranga Māori, with multiple forms and uses.

work_or_witness: Traditional Māori religion – ngā karakia a te Māori; Whakapapa – genealogy · ‘Spiritual concepts’, § ‘Mana’, para. 1
definition: The cited reference describes mana as extraordinary power, essence, or presence, relating to authority, power, and prestige, and ties it closely to tapu.
cultural_caution: Do not translate mana into a game resource, numerical power meter, or generic magical energy; its meanings are contextual and relational.

supports: The cited definition of mana and its relationship to tapu.

work_or_witness: Traditional Māori religion – ngā karakia a te Māori; Whakapapa – genealogy · ‘Spiritual concepts’, § ‘Tapu and noa’, paras. 1–3
definition: The cited reference describes inherited and other tapu as affecting people, flora, fauna, and objects and as carrying restrictions on behaviour.
cultural_caution: Do not render tapu as a simple taboo flag, alignment rule, or status effect. Restrictions and practices require local, relational, and appropriate cultural context.

supports: The cited reference describes tapu and the restrictions associated with it.

work_or_witness: Māori Mythology · ‘Rituals and ceremonies’, § ‘Tapu removal’, paras. 1–2
literal_gloss: ordinary, common, or free from restriction
definition: The cited reference glosses noa as ordinary, common, or free from the restrictions or rules of tapu, and records practices of making a person or thing noa.
cultural_caution: Noa is not a generic ‘nonmagical’ or neutral game state, and it should not be detached from tapu, tikanga, and the particular context of its use.

supports: The page defines rituals that remove tapu and make a person or thing noa.

work_or_witness: Whenua – how the land was shaped · ‘The North and South islands’, §§ ‘Māui fishes up the North Island’, ‘How the North Island got its shape’, and ‘Māui and Nukutaimemeha’, paras. 1–5
definition: Name for the North Island in the selected Māui fishing account; the cited page also records divergent regional accounts of Māui’s canoe and the land’s form.
cultural_caution: This is sacred and relational geography, not a generic fantasy map feature or an evidence-free claim about all Māori land traditions. Keep the cited Ngāti Porou and Ngāti Toarangatira variants visible.

citations.locator: ‘The North and South islands’, §§ ‘Māui fishes up the North Island’, ‘How the North Island got its shape’, and ‘Māui and Nukutaimemeha’, paras. 1–5
supports: Te Ika-a-Māui is named in the Māui land-form account and the page specifies regional variation.

work_or_witness: Māori Mythology · ‘Māui’, § ‘Māui’, para. 1; Māori Mythology · ‘Whakapapa with links to Polynesia’, § ‘Culture hero sequences’, paras. 1–3
literal_gloss: proper name; no literal gloss asserted
definition: Te Ara describes Māui as a great trickster hero and its whakapapa reference calls Māui-centred cycles culture-hero sequences; the records limit this label to the cited published descriptions.
cultural_caution: ‘Culture hero’ and ‘trickster hero’ are analytical English labels, not Māori character classes. Māui’s genealogical position and narratives vary between tribal traditions and across Polynesia.

supports: Te Ara calls Māui a great trickster hero.

citations.locator: ‘Whakapapa with links to Polynesia’, § ‘Culture hero sequences’, paras. 1–3
supports: Te Ara identifies Māui-centred cycles as culture-hero sequences and states that genealogical sequences vary widely.

literal_gloss: proper name; no literal gloss asserted
definition: Name used in the cited reference account for Hinetītama after she flees to the underworld; the character record keeps this as an account-specific change of name/state.
cultural_caution: Do not generalize this named narrative change into a transformation power, death class, or universal Māori afterlife model.

supports: The cited account says Hinetītama fled to the underworld and became Hine-nui-te-pō.
